Section

On mentioning some of the lessons and benefits contained in this great story, about which Allah said at its beginning ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, and said ﴿Certainly in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask﴾, and said at its end ﴿Certainly in their stories is a lesson for those of understanding﴾, apart from the benefits already mentioned within its folds.

Among them: this story is among the best and clearest and most explicit of stories, because of the varieties of transitions it contains: from one state to another, from trial to trial, from trial to bounty and favor, from humiliation to honor, from slavery to kingship, from separation and dispersal to gathering and harmony, from grief to joy, from plenty to drought, from drought to plenty, from constriction to ease, and from denial to acknowledgment. Blessed is the One who related it and made it the best, clearest, and most explicit.

Among them: it contains a foundation for the interpretation of dreams (ta'bir al-ru'ya). The science of interpretation is one of the important sciences that Allah gives to whomever He wills of His servants. Most of what it is built upon is correspondence and resemblance in name and attribute.

As for Joseph's dream, in which he saw the sun, the moon, and eleven stars prostrating to him, the point of correspondence is that these lights are the adornment of the sky and its beauty, and in them are its benefits. Likewise, the prophets and scholars are an adornment and beauty of the earth, and by them one is guided through darkness just as one is guided by these lights. And because the root is his father and mother, while his brothers are the branches, it is fitting that the root be greater in light and size than what is derived from it. Therefore the sun was his mother, the moon his father, and the stars his brothers. Another point of correspondence is that the word "sun" is feminine, so it was his mother, while the moon and the stars are masculine, so they were his father and brothers. Another point of correspondence is that the one who prostrates honors and reveres the one prostrated to, and the one prostrated to is honored and revered. Therefore this indicates that Joseph would be honored and revered by his parents and brothers. It follows from this that he would be chosen and preferred in knowledge and in the virtues that necessitate that, and for this reason his father said to him ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events﴾.

As for the resemblance in the dream of the two young men: the one who saw that he was pressing wine was interpreted by what it would lead to, that he would give his lord a drink, and that includes his release from prison. The one who saw that he was carrying bread on his head, of which birds were eating, was interpreted by the fact that the scalp, flesh, and what is in it of brain belonged to him, that he would be carried, and that he would be exposed to the birds in a place where they could eat from his head. He saw from his condition that he would be killed and crucified, and after his death be exposed to the birds, which would eat from his head, and this could only happen by crucifixion after killing.

The king's dream of the cows and the ears of grain was interpreted as years of abundance and years of drought. The point of correspondence is that the welfare of subjects is tied to the king, and their interests depend on him: by his soundness they are sound and by his corruption they are corrupted. Likewise, the years are the means by which the subjects' conditions are good and their livelihood is stable or not. As for cows, the land is plowed with them and water is drawn with them, and when the year is fertile they grow fat, and when it is barren they become lean. Likewise, ears of grain increase and turn green in abundance, and decrease and dry up in drought, and they are the best of the land's crops.

Among them: the evidences it contains for the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), since he related to his people this long story though he had not read the books of the ancients, nor studied with anyone whom his people saw among them morning and evening. He was unlettered, neither writing nor reading, and it agrees with what is in the earlier scriptures. And they were not present when they resolved upon their plan while they were scheming.

Among them: one should keep away from the causes of evil and conceal what its harm is feared from. This is from Jacob's saying to Joseph ﴿My son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot against you a plot﴾.

Among them: it is permissible to mention a person in a way he dislikes for the sake of advising another, from His saying ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾.

Among them: Allah's blessing upon a servant is a blessing upon those connected to him from his household, relatives, and companions, and it may encompass them so that what happened to him happens to them because of him. As Jacob said in interpreting Joseph's dream ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob﴾. When the blessing was completed for Joseph, there came to the family of Jacob the honor, establishment in the land, joy, and happiness that came about because of Joseph.

Among them: justice is required in all matters, not only in the ruler's treatment of his subjects or in what is below that, but even in a father's treatment of his children in love, preference, and other things. Neglecting this disturbs affairs and corrupts conditions. For this reason, when Jacob preferred Joseph in love and favored him over his brothers, what happened from them happened to themselves, to their father, and to their brother.

Among them: caution against the evil consequences of sins, and that one sin entails many sins, and the sinner does not complete it except through several crimes. When Joseph's brothers wanted to separate him from his father, they resorted to various tricks, lied several times, and deceived their father regarding the shirt and the blood on it, and regarding their coming in the evening weeping. Do not think it unlikely that much inquiry was made about this during that period, and perhaps it reached the point where they gathered before Joseph. Whenever the inquiry arose, lies and fabrications were uttered as they were. This is the evil of sin and its consequent and preceding effects.

Among them: the lesson in a servant's condition is in the perfection of the end, not in the deficiency of the beginning. The sons of Jacob, peace be upon them, did what they did at the outset, which was among the greatest causes of deficiency and blame. Then their matter ended in sincere repentance and complete forgiveness from Joseph and from their father, and prayers for them for forgiveness and mercy. When a servant forgoes his right, Allah is the best of the merciful. For this reason, according to the most correct opinions, they were prophets, based on His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes﴾. They are the twelve sons of Jacob and their descendants. Among what indicates this is that in Joseph's dream he saw them as shining stars, and stars contain light and guidance, which are among the attributes of the prophets. If they were not prophets, they were scholars and guiding leaders.

Among them: what Allah bestowed upon Joseph, peace be upon him, of knowledge, forbearance, noble character, calling to Allah and to His religion, and his pardon of his erring brothers, a pardon he hastened to give them and completed by not reproaching them or upbraiding them for it. Then his great kindness to his parents and his benevolence to his brothers, and indeed to all creatures.

Among them: some evil is lighter than other evil, and committing the lesser of two harms is better than committing the greater of them. When Joseph's brothers agreed to kill Joseph or throw him onto the ground, and one of them said ﴿Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the bottom of the well﴾, his saying was better and lighter than theirs, and because of it the great sin was lightened for his brothers.

Among them: when a thing has passed through many hands and has become part of the property, and it is not known to have been obtained in a manner contrary to the Shariah, then there is no sin on whoever handles it by sale, purchase, service, benefit, or use. Joseph, peace be upon him, was sold by his brothers in a forbidden sale that was not permissible. Then the caravan carried him off to Egypt, where they sold him, and he remained with his master as a servant and slave, though Allah called him "master," and among them he was in the position of an honored slave.

Among them: caution against seclusion with women, which may lead to temptation, and caution also against love whose harm is feared. The wife of the Aziz did what she did because of being alone with Joseph and her intense love for him, which did not leave her until she solicited him with that solicitation, and then lied about him, so he was imprisoned for a long time because of her.

Among them: the concern that Joseph had regarding the woman, and then his leaving it for the sake of Allah, is among the things that raise him to Allah in nearness. Concern is a call of the commanding soul to evil, and it is the nature of most of creation. When he weighed it against the love of Allah and fear of Him, the love of Allah and fear of Him overcame the call of the soul and desire. Thus he was among those who ﴿feared the standing before their Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾. And among the seven whom Allah shades under the shadow of His Throne on a day when there is no shade but His: one of them is a man whom a woman of position and beauty invited, and he said, "I fear Allah." The concern for which a servant is blamed is the concern that dwells within him and becomes a resolve, which may be joined by action.

Among them: whoever faith has entered his heart, and who is sincere to Allah in all his affairs, Allah will repel from him by the proof of his faith and the truthfulness of his sincerity every kind of evil and immorality and causes of sin, as a recompense for his faith and sincerity. This is based on His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our sincere servants﴾, according to the reading of those who read the lam with a kasra (the mukhlis, "sincere," being the one who purified himself). According to the one who reads it with a fatha, it is from Allah's making him sincere, and it includes his own sincerity by himself. When he made his deed sincere for Allah, Allah made him sincere and purified him from evil and immorality.

Among them: when a servant sees a place in which there is temptation and causes of disobedience, he should flee from it and run away as far as he can, so that he may be able to free himself from disobedience. When Joseph, peace be upon him, was solicited by the one in whose house he was, he fled running toward the door to free himself from her evil.

Among them: indications are acted upon when there is ambiguity. If a man and his wife dispute over some household utensil, then what is suitable for the man belongs to the man, and what is suitable for the woman belongs to her, if there is no evidence. Likewise, if a carpenter and a blacksmith dispute over the tools of their trade without evidence. Acting upon qafah (the expertise of tracing and recognizing resemblances and traces) in matters of resemblance and traces also falls under this principle. The witness of Joseph testified by the indication and ruled by it, regarding the tearing of the shirt, and he inferred from its tearing from behind the truthfulness of Joseph and the lying of her. Among what indicates this principle is that he deduced from the finding of the drinking cup in his brother's baggage the ruling that he was a thief, without a witness's testimony or confession. Therefore, if the stolen item is found in the thief's possession, especially if he is known for theft, he is ruled a thief, and this is stronger than testimony. Likewise, a man found vomiting wine, or a woman who has no husband or master found pregnant, is subjected to the prescribed punishment, unless an impediment prevents it. For this reason Allah called this ruling a witness, saying ﴿And a witness from her family testified﴾.

Among them: the apparent and inner beauty that Joseph possessed. His outward beauty caused in the woman in whose house he was what it caused, and in the women whom she gathered when they blamed her for it, so that they cut their hands and said ﴿This is not a human; this is none but a noble angel﴾. As for his inner beauty, it is his great chastity from disobedience despite the many motives for committing it, and the testimony of the Aziz's wife and the women afterward to his innocence. For this reason the Aziz's wife said ﴿And I certainly solicited him, but he refused﴾, and said afterward ﴿Now the truth has become evident. I solicited him, and he is certainly of the truthful﴾, and the women said ﴿Far be Allah [from imperfection]! We know no evil of him﴾.

Among them: Joseph, peace be upon him, chose prison over disobedience. Thus a servant, when he is tested between two matters, either committing a sin or a worldly punishment, should choose the worldly punishment over committing the sin that requires severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter. For this reason, among the signs of faith is that a servant hates to return to disbelief after Allah has rescued him from it, just as he hates to be thrown into the Fire.

Among them: a servant should seek refuge in Allah and take shelter in His protection when the causes of disobedience are present, and disclaim his own power and strength. This is based on Joseph's saying, peace be upon him, ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾.

Among them: knowledge and intellect call their possessor to good and forbid him from evil, while ignorance calls its possessor to following the desire of the soul, even if it is disobedience and harmful to its possessor.

Among them: just as a servant has worship of Allah in ease, he also has worship in hardship. Joseph, peace be upon him, never stopped calling to Allah. When he entered prison he continued in that, and he called the two young men to monotheism and forbade them from polytheism. Among his acuteness, peace be upon him, was that when he saw in them a readiness for his call, since they had a good opinion of him and said to him ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers﴾, and came to him so that he would interpret their dreams, he saw them eager for its interpretation from him. He considered this an opportunity and seized it, calling them to Allah, may He be exalted, before interpreting their dreams, so that this would be more successful for his aim and closer to attaining his objective. He first explained to them that what brought him to the condition in which they saw him, of perfection and knowledge, was his faith and monotheism and his abandonment of the creed of those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day. This was a call to them through condition, then he called them through speech, explaining the corruption of polytheism and proving it, and the reality of monotheism and proving it.

Among them: one begins with what is most important and then what is next. When a mufti is asked, and the questioner's need is greater than what he asked about, it is fitting that he teach him what he needs before answering his question. This is a sign of the teacher's sincerity, acuteness, and good guidance and instruction. When the two young men asked Joseph about the dream, he first presented to them, before interpreting it, his call to Allah alone, with no partner.

Among them: whoever falls into a disliked and difficult situation, there is no harm in seeking help from someone who has the ability to free him or to convey his condition. This is not a complaint to a creature, since it is among the ordinary matters through which people customarily help one another. For this reason Joseph said to the one of the two young men whom he thought would be saved ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾.

Among the lessons drawn from this story: it is recommended, and indeed strongly required, that the teacher (*mu'allim*) teach with complete sincerity. He should not make his teaching a means of exchange for anyone's wealth, status, or benefit. He should not refuse to teach, or withhold sincere advice, when the questioner fails to do what the teacher assigned him. Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to one of the two young men, who had been asked to mention him to his lord, "Mention me to your lord," but the man forgot and did not mention him. When the people's need for Yusuf's help became apparent, they sent that same young man, who came to him asking for a ruling (*fatwa*) about that dream. Yusuf did not rebuke him or reproach him for failing to mention him. Instead, he answered the question fully and completely in every respect.

Another lesson: the one who is asked should direct the questioner to something beneficial related to his question, and guide him to the path by which he may benefit in his religion and his worldly life. This is part of the perfection of sincere advice, insight, and good guidance. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not limit himself to interpreting the king's dream. He also showed them, in addition, what they should do in those fertile years of abundant crops and large harvests.

Another lesson: a person is not blamed for striving to remove an accusation from himself and to seek vindication for it; rather, he is praised for doing so. Yusuf refused to leave the prison until his innocence was made clear by the state of the women who had cut their hands.

Another lesson: the virtue of knowledge, including knowledge of the rulings and the Sharia, knowledge of dream interpretation, and knowledge of management and upbringing. Knowledge is better than outward beauty, even if that beauty reaches the level of Yusuf's beauty. Yusuf's beauty brought him that trial and imprisonment, while his knowledge brought him honour, elevation, and firm establishment in the land. Every good in this world and the Hereafter is a consequence and necessary result of knowledge.

Another lesson: the knowledge of interpreting dreams (*ta'bir al-ru'ya*) is among the Sharia sciences, and a person is rewarded for learning and teaching it. Dream interpretation falls under giving a ruling (*fatwa*), as shown by His words to the two young men, "The matter about which you both seek a ruling has been decided" (﴿قُضِيَ الأمرُ الذي فيه تستفتيان﴾). The king said, "Give me a ruling about my dream" (﴿أفتوني في رؤيايَ﴾), and the young man said to Yusuf, "Give us a ruling about seven fat cows..." (﴿أفۡتِنا في سبع بقراتٍ﴾), and the verses that follow. Therefore, it is not permissible to undertake interpreting a dream without knowledge.

Another lesson: there is no harm in a person describing what he has of the attributes of perfection, whether in knowledge or in action, when there is a benefit in doing so, provided he does not intend showing off (*riya'*) and remains free of falsehood. Yusuf said, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian" (﴿اجعَلۡني على خزائن الأرض إنِّي حفيظٌ عليمٌ﴾).

Likewise, holding public office is not blameworthy when the one who holds it fulfils, to the extent of his ability, the rights of God and the rights of His servants. There is no harm in seeking it when the one seeking it is more qualified than others. What is blameworthy is seeking office when one lacks the competence for it, or when someone else of similar or higher standing exists, or when one does not intend by it to establish the command of God. For these reasons, seeking office and exposing oneself to it are forbidden.

Another lesson: God is vast in generosity and munificence. He bestows upon His servant the good of this world and the Hereafter. The good of the Hereafter has two causes: faith (*iman*) and piety (*taqwa*). It is better than the reward and possession of this world. A servant should encourage his soul and make it long for God's reward, and should not let it grieve when it sees the people of this world and their pleasures while it is unable to obtain them. Rather, he should console it with God's reward in the Hereafter and His great bounty, as He says, "And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of God" (﴿ولأجۡرُ الآخرة خيرٌ للذين آمنوا وكانوا يتَّقون﴾).

Another lesson: collecting provisions and food is permissible when its aim is to extend provision to people without harming them. Yusuf commanded them to gather grain and food in the fertile years in preparation for the lean years. This does not contradict reliance upon God (*tawakkul*). Rather, the servant relies upon God while also acting upon the means that benefit him in his religion and his worldly life.

Another lesson: the excellent management of Yusuf when he took charge of the storehouses of the land, so that the stores of grain became very abundant. People from distant regions came to Egypt seeking provisions, because they knew the grain was plentiful there. He would not measure out to anyone more than the amount of their specific need, or less than that, and he did not give any arrival more than the measure of a camel's load.

Another lesson: the legitimacy of hospitality (*diyafa*), that it is one of the traditions of the messengers, and that honouring the guest is recommended. This is shown by Yusuf's words to his brothers, "Do you not see that I give full measure, and that I am the best of hosts?" (﴿ألا تَرَوۡنَ أنِّي أوفي الكيل وأنا خيرُ المنزِلينَ﴾).

Another lesson: having bad thoughts (*su' al-zann*) when there are clear indications for them is not forbidden or prohibited. Jacob refused to send Yusuf with them until they pressed him very hard, and then, after they came to him and claimed that a wolf had devoured Yusuf, he said, "Rather, your souls have beautified a matter for you" (﴿بل سوَّلت لكم أنفسُكم أمراً﴾). He said to them about the other brother, "Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?" (﴿هل آمَنُكُم عليه إلاَّ كما أمِنتُكم على أخيه من قبل﴾). Then, when Yusuf detained his brother with him and his brothers came to their father without him, he said to them, "Rather, your souls have beautified a matter for you" (﴿بل سوَّلَتۡ لكم أنفسُكم أمراً﴾). In this latter case, although they were not negligent, what had occurred from them made it necessary for their father to say what he said, without sin or blame upon him.

Another lesson: using means that ward off the evil eye and other harms, or that remove them after they have befallen, is not forbidden but permissible, even though nothing happens except by God's decree and predestination (*qada' wa qadar*). Means are themselves part of God's decree and predestination. This is shown by Jacob's command to his sons, "O my sons, do not enter by one gate, but enter by different gates" (﴿يا بنيَّ لا تدخُلوا من بابٍ واحدٍ وادخلوا من أبواب متفرقة﴾).

Another lesson: the permissibility of using stratagems (*makayid*) by which rights may be attained. Knowing hidden methods that lead to one's goals is praiseworthy for the servant. What is forbidden is only devising a way to cancel an obligation or to commit a prohibited act.

Another lesson: a person who wishes to give another the impression of something he does not want the other to know should use indirect speech, whether verbal or practical (*ma'arid*), which prevents him from lying. This is what Yusuf did when he placed the bowl in his brother's bag, then took it out, giving the impression that he was a thief, while there was nothing in it except an indication that suggested this to his brothers. Afterwards he said, "God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property" (﴿معاذَ الله أن نأخُذَ إلاَّ مَن وجدنا متاعنا عنده﴾). He did not say, "Whoever stole our property," nor did he say, "We found our property with him." Rather, he used a general statement that suits him and others. There is no prohibition in this. It only gives the impression that he is a thief, in order to achieve the immediate aim, which was that his brother would remain with him. This false impression was removed from the brother after the situation became clear.

Another lesson: a person may testify only to what he knows and has verified, either through direct observation or through the report of someone he trusts and whose report reassures the soul. This is shown by their words, "We bear witness only to what we know" (﴿وما شَهِدۡنا إلا بما علمنا﴾).

Another lesson: this great trial by which God tested His prophet and chosen one, Jacob, peace be upon him. God decreed that he be separated from his son Yusuf, whom he could not bear to be parted from even for one hour, and this separation grieved him most intensely. The separation lasted a long time, not less than thirty years, and sorrow never left Jacob's heart during that period. "His eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing it" (﴿وابيضَّتۡ عيناه من الحزنِ فهو كظيمٌ﴾). Then the matter grew even more severe when he was separated from his second son, Yusuf's full brother. Yet he remained patient with God's command, seeking his reward from God. He had pledged to himself beautiful patience, and there is no doubt that he fulfilled what he pledged. His words, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God" (﴿إنَّما أشكو بثِّي وحزني إلى الله﴾), do not contradict this, for complaining to God does not contradict patience. What contradicts it is complaining to created beings.

Another lesson: relief comes with distress, and with hardship comes ease. When Jacob's grief lasted long and grew intense to its utmost limit, and then the family of Jacob fell into dire need and harm touched them, God then permitted relief. The reunion came at the most critical time of their need and necessity, so the reward was completed and joy came. It is known from this that God tests His friends with hardship and ease, with adversity and prosperity, in order to test their patience and gratitude, and thereby their faith, certainty, and knowledge of Him increase.

Another lesson: a person may inform others of what he is experiencing, such as illness, poverty, or similar things, without complaining bitterly (*tasakhkhut*). Yusuf's brothers said, "O Chief, adversity has afflicted us and our family" (﴿يا أيُّها العزيز مسَّنا وأهلَنا الضرُّ﴾), and Yusuf did not object to them.

Another lesson: the virtue of piety and patience, and that every good in this world and the Hereafter is a consequence of piety and patience, and that the outcome for those who possess them is the best outcome. This is shown by His words, "God has been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever is mindful of God and patient, God does not waste the reward of the doers of good" (﴿قد منَّ الله علينا إنَّه من يتَّقِ ويَصۡبِرۡ فإنَّ الله لا يضيع أجر المحسنين﴾).

Another lesson: whoever has been blessed by God with a blessing after hardship, poverty, and a bad condition should acknowledge God's blessing upon him and should not stop remembering his former state, so that this remembrance produces gratitude whenever he recalls it. This is shown by Yusuf's words, peace be upon him, "He was good to me when He brought me out of prison and brought you from the desert" (﴿وقد أحسنَ بي إذ أخرَجَني من السجن وجاء بكم من البَدۡوِ﴾).

Another lesson: the great kindness of God toward Yusuf, in that He transferred him through those conditions and brought him hardships and trials, so that through them He might bring him to the highest goals and the loftiest ranks.

Another lesson: a servant should constantly turn to God, seeking to have his faith firmly established, should adopt the means that bring this about, and should ask God for a good ending and the completion of His blessing. This is shown by the words of Yusuf, peace be upon him, "My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom and taught me the interpretation of dreams. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Let me die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous" (﴿ربِّي قد آتَيۡتَني من الملك وعلَّمۡتني من تأويل الأحاديث فاطر السمواتِ والأرض أنتَ وليِّي في الدُّنيا والآخرة توفَّني مسلماً وألحقۡني بالصَّالحين﴾).

This is what God has facilitated of benefits and lessons in this blessed story. Surely other things will become apparent to the one who reflects and contemplates. We ask Him, exalted is He, for beneficial knowledge and accepted deeds, for He is Generous and Bountiful.

The commentary on Surah Yusuf, and his father and brothers, peace be upon them, is complete. All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds.

{110} He, may He be exalted, informs that He sends noble messengers, and the wicked, base people reject them. Allah gives those people respite so that they may return to the truth. Allah continues to give them respite until the situation reaches an extreme of hardship for the messengers. Even though the messengers have perfect certainty and firm belief in Allah's promise and threat, a kind of despair and a kind of weakening of knowledge and conviction may occur to their hearts. When the matter reaches this state, ﴿Then Our help came to them, and whom We willed was saved﴾: they are the messengers and their followers. ﴿And Our punishment is not averted from the criminal people﴾; that is, Our punishment is not averted from those who committed crimes and dared against Allah, so they have no power and no helper.

{111} ﴿Certainly in their stories﴾; that is, in the stories of the prophets and messengers with their peoples ﴿is a lesson for those of understanding﴾; that is, they take lessons from them, both the people of goodness and the people of evil, and that whoever does as they did will receive what they received, whether honor or humiliation. They also take lessons from what belongs to Allah of perfect attributes and great wisdom, and that He is Allah, to whom worship is due alone, with no partner. And His saying ﴿it was not a narration invented﴾; that is, this Qur'an, through which Allah related to you the reports of the unseen, was not a narration fabricated and invented like the false tales. ﴿But﴾ it was ﴿a confirmation of what was before it﴾: of the earlier scriptures, agreeing with them and bearing witness to their soundness, ﴿and a detailed explanation of all things﴾: which the servants need from the foundations and branches of religion, and from proofs and evidences. ﴿And guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾: for by means of what they gain from it of knowledge of the truth and preference for it, guidance is attained for them, and by the immediate and deferred reward they receive, mercy is attained for them.

Section

On mentioning some of the lessons and benefits contained in this great story, about which Allah said at its beginning ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, and said ﴿Certainly in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask﴾, and said at its end ﴿Certainly in their stories is a lesson for those of understanding﴾, apart from the benefits already mentioned within its folds.

Among them: this story is among the best and clearest and most explicit of stories, because of the varieties of transitions it contains: from one state to another, from trial to trial, from trial to bounty and favor, from humiliation to honor, from slavery to kingship, from separation and dispersal to gathering and harmony, from grief to joy, from plenty to drought, from drought to plenty, from constriction to ease, and from denial to acknowledgment. Blessed is the One who related it and made it the best, clearest, and most explicit.

Among them: it contains a foundation for the interpretation of dreams (ta'bir al-ru'ya). The science of interpretation is one of the important sciences that Allah gives to whomever He wills of His servants. Most of what it is built upon is correspondence and resemblance in name and attribute.

As for Joseph's dream, in which he saw the sun, the moon, and eleven stars prostrating to him, the point of correspondence is that these lights are the adornment of the sky and its beauty, and in them are its benefits. Likewise, the prophets and scholars are an adornment and beauty of the earth, and by them one is guided through darkness just as one is guided by these lights. And because the root is his father and mother, while his brothers are the branches, it is fitting that the root be greater in light and size than what is derived from it. Therefore the sun was his mother, the moon his father, and the stars his brothers. Another point of correspondence is that the word "sun" is feminine, so it was his mother, while the moon and the stars are masculine, so they were his father and brothers. Another point of correspondence is that the one who prostrates honors and reveres the one prostrated to, and the one prostrated to is honored and revered. Therefore this indicates that Joseph would be honored and revered by his parents and brothers. It follows from this that he would be chosen and preferred in knowledge and in the virtues that necessitate that, and for this reason his father said to him ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events﴾.

As for the resemblance in the dream of the two young men: the one who saw that he was pressing wine was interpreted by what it would lead to, that he would give his lord a drink, and that includes his release from prison. The one who saw that he was carrying bread on his head, of which birds were eating, was interpreted by the fact that the scalp, flesh, and what is in it of brain belonged to him, that he would be carried, and that he would be exposed to the birds in a place where they could eat from his head. He saw from his condition that he would be killed and crucified, and after his death be exposed to the birds, which would eat from his head, and this could only happen by crucifixion after killing.

The king's dream of the cows and the ears of grain was interpreted as years of abundance and years of drought. The point of correspondence is that the welfare of subjects is tied to the king, and their interests depend on him: by his soundness they are sound and by his corruption they are corrupted. Likewise, the years are the means by which the subjects' conditions are good and their livelihood is stable or not. As for cows, the land is plowed with them and water is drawn with them, and when the year is fertile they grow fat, and when it is barren they become lean. Likewise, ears of grain increase and turn green in abundance, and decrease and dry up in drought, and they are the best of the land's crops.

Among them: the evidences it contains for the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), since he related to his people this long story though he had not read the books of the ancients, nor studied with anyone whom his people saw among them morning and evening. He was unlettered, neither writing nor reading, and it agrees with what is in the earlier scriptures. And they were not present when they resolved upon their plan while they were scheming.

Among them: one should keep away from the causes of evil and conceal what its harm is feared from. This is from Jacob's saying to Joseph ﴿My son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot against you a plot﴾.

Among them: it is permissible to mention a person in a way he dislikes for the sake of advising another, from His saying ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾.

Among them: Allah's blessing upon a servant is a blessing upon those connected to him from his household, relatives, and companions, and it may encompass them so that what happened to him happens to them because of him. As Jacob said in interpreting Joseph's dream ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob﴾. When the blessing was completed for Joseph, there came to the family of Jacob the honor, establishment in the land, joy, and happiness that came about because of Joseph.

Among them: justice is required in all matters, not only in the ruler's treatment of his subjects or in what is below that, but even in a father's treatment of his children in love, preference, and other things. Neglecting this disturbs affairs and corrupts conditions. For this reason, when Jacob preferred Joseph in love and favored him over his brothers, what happened from them happened to themselves, to their father, and to their brother.

Among them: caution against the evil consequences of sins, and that one sin entails many sins, and the sinner does not complete it except through several crimes. When Joseph's brothers wanted to separate him from his father, they resorted to various tricks, lied several times, and deceived their father regarding the shirt and the blood on it, and regarding their coming in the evening weeping. Do not think it unlikely that much inquiry was made about this during that period, and perhaps it reached the point where they gathered before Joseph. Whenever the inquiry arose, lies and fabrications were uttered as they were. This is the evil of sin and its consequent and preceding effects.

Among them: the lesson in a servant's condition is in the perfection of the end, not in the deficiency of the beginning. The sons of Jacob, peace be upon them, did what they did at the outset, which was among the greatest causes of deficiency and blame. Then their matter ended in sincere repentance and complete forgiveness from Joseph and from their father, and prayers for them for forgiveness and mercy. When a servant forgoes his right, Allah is the best of the merciful. For this reason, according to the most correct opinions, they were prophets, based on His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes﴾. They are the twelve sons of Jacob and their descendants. Among what indicates this is that in Joseph's dream he saw them as shining stars, and stars contain light and guidance, which are among the attributes of the prophets. If they were not prophets, they were scholars and guiding leaders.

Among them: what Allah bestowed upon Joseph, peace be upon him, of knowledge, forbearance, noble character, calling to Allah and to His religion, and his pardon of his erring brothers, a pardon he hastened to give them and completed by not reproaching them or upbraiding them for it. Then his great kindness to his parents and his benevolence to his brothers, and indeed to all creatures.

Among them: some evil is lighter than other evil, and committing the lesser of two harms is better than committing the greater of them. When Joseph's brothers agreed to kill Joseph or throw him onto the ground, and one of them said ﴿Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the bottom of the well﴾, his saying was better and lighter than theirs, and because of it the great sin was lightened for his brothers.

Among them: when a thing has passed through many hands and has become part of the property, and it is not known to have been obtained in a manner contrary to the Shariah, then there is no sin on whoever handles it by sale, purchase, service, benefit, or use. Joseph, peace be upon him, was sold by his brothers in a forbidden sale that was not permissible. Then the caravan carried him off to Egypt, where they sold him, and he remained with his master as a servant and slave, though Allah called him "master," and among them he was in the position of an honored slave.

Among them: caution against seclusion with women, which may lead to temptation, and caution also against love whose harm is feared. The wife of the Aziz did what she did because of being alone with Joseph and her intense love for him, which did not leave her until she solicited him with that solicitation, and then lied about him, so he was imprisoned for a long time because of her.

Among them: the concern that Joseph had regarding the woman, and then his leaving it for the sake of Allah, is among the things that raise him to Allah in nearness. Concern is a call of the commanding soul to evil, and it is the nature of most of creation. When he weighed it against the love of Allah and fear of Him, the love of Allah and fear of Him overcame the call of the soul and desire. Thus he was among those who ﴿feared the standing before their Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾. And among the seven whom Allah shades under the shadow of His Throne on a day when there is no shade but His: one of them is a man whom a woman of position and beauty invited, and he said, "I fear Allah." The concern for which a servant is blamed is the concern that dwells within him and becomes a resolve, which may be joined by action.

Among them: whoever faith has entered his heart, and who is sincere to Allah in all his affairs, Allah will repel from him by the proof of his faith and the truthfulness of his sincerity every kind of evil and immorality and causes of sin, as a recompense for his faith and sincerity. This is based on His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our sincere servants﴾, according to the reading of those who read the lam with a kasra (the mukhlis, "sincere," being the one who purified himself). According to the one who reads it with a fatha, it is from Allah's making him sincere, and it includes his own sincerity by himself. When he made his deed sincere for Allah, Allah made him sincere and purified him from evil and immorality.

Among them: when a servant sees a place in which there is temptation and causes of disobedience, he should flee from it and run away as far as he can, so that he may be able to free himself from disobedience. When Joseph, peace be upon him, was solicited by the one in whose house he was, he fled running toward the door to free himself from her evil.

Among them: indications are acted upon when there is ambiguity. If a man and his wife dispute over some household utensil, then what is suitable for the man belongs to the man, and what is suitable for the woman belongs to her, if there is no evidence. Likewise, if a carpenter and a blacksmith dispute over the tools of their trade without evidence. Acting upon qafah (the expertise of tracing and recognizing resemblances and traces) in matters of resemblance and traces also falls under this principle. The witness of Joseph testified by the indication and ruled by it, regarding the tearing of the shirt, and he inferred from its tearing from behind the truthfulness of Joseph and the lying of her. Among what indicates this principle is that he deduced from the finding of the drinking cup in his brother's baggage the ruling that he was a thief, without a witness's testimony or confession. Therefore, if the stolen item is found in the thief's possession, especially if he is known for theft, he is ruled a thief, and this is stronger than testimony. Likewise, a man found vomiting wine, or a woman who has no husband or master found pregnant, is subjected to the prescribed punishment, unless an impediment prevents it. For this reason Allah called this ruling a witness, saying ﴿And a witness from her family testified﴾.

Among them: the apparent and inner beauty that Joseph possessed. His outward beauty caused in the woman in whose house he was what it caused, and in the women whom she gathered when they blamed her for it, so that they cut their hands and said ﴿This is not a human; this is none but a noble angel﴾. As for his inner beauty, it is his great chastity from disobedience despite the many motives for committing it, and the testimony of the Aziz's wife and the women afterward to his innocence. For this reason the Aziz's wife said ﴿And I certainly solicited him, but he refused﴾, and said afterward ﴿Now the truth has become evident. I solicited him, and he is certainly of the truthful﴾, and the women said ﴿Far be Allah [from imperfection]! We know no evil of him﴾.

Among them: Joseph, peace be upon him, chose prison over disobedience. Thus a servant, when he is tested between two matters, either committing a sin or a worldly punishment, should choose the worldly punishment over committing the sin that requires severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter. For this reason, among the signs of faith is that a servant hates to return to disbelief after Allah has rescued him from it, just as he hates to be thrown into the Fire.

Among them: a servant should seek refuge in Allah and take shelter in His protection when the causes of disobedience are present, and disclaim his own power and strength. This is based on Joseph's saying, peace be upon him, ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾.

Among them: knowledge and intellect call their possessor to good and forbid him from evil, while ignorance calls its possessor to following the desire of the soul, even if it is disobedience and harmful to its possessor.

Among them: just as a servant has worship of Allah in ease, he also has worship in hardship. Joseph, peace be upon him, never stopped calling to Allah. When he entered prison he continued in that, and he called the two young men to monotheism and forbade them from polytheism. Among his acuteness, peace be upon him, was that when he saw in them a readiness for his call, since they had a good opinion of him and said to him ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers﴾, and came to him so that he would interpret their dreams, he saw them eager for its interpretation from him. He considered this an opportunity and seized it, calling them to Allah, may He be exalted, before interpreting their dreams, so that this would be more successful for his aim and closer to attaining his objective. He first explained to them that what brought him to the condition in which they saw him, of perfection and knowledge, was his faith and monotheism and his abandonment of the creed of those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day. This was a call to them through condition, then he called them through speech, explaining the corruption of polytheism and proving it, and the reality of monotheism and proving it.

Among them: one begins with what is most important and then what is next. When a mufti is asked, and the questioner's need is greater than what he asked about, it is fitting that he teach him what he needs before answering his question. This is a sign of the teacher's sincerity, acuteness, and good guidance and instruction. When the two young men asked Joseph about the dream, he first presented to them, before interpreting it, his call to Allah alone, with no partner.

Among them: whoever falls into a disliked and difficult situation, there is no harm in seeking help from someone who has the ability to free him or to convey his condition. This is not a complaint to a creature, since it is among the ordinary matters through which people customarily help one another. For this reason Joseph said to the one of the two young men whom he thought would be saved ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾.

Among the lessons drawn from this story: it is recommended, and indeed strongly required, that the teacher (*mu'allim*) teach with complete sincerity. He should not make his teaching a means of exchange for anyone's wealth, status, or benefit. He should not refuse to teach, or withhold sincere advice, when the questioner fails to do what the teacher assigned him. Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to one of the two young men, who had been asked to mention him to his lord, "Mention me to your lord," but the man forgot and did not mention him. When the people's need for Yusuf's help became apparent, they sent that same young man, who came to him asking for a ruling (*fatwa*) about that dream. Yusuf did not rebuke him or reproach him for failing to mention him. Instead, he answered the question fully and completely in every respect.

Another lesson: the one who is asked should direct the questioner to something beneficial related to his question, and guide him to the path by which he may benefit in his religion and his worldly life. This is part of the perfection of sincere advice, insight, and good guidance. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not limit himself to interpreting the king's dream. He also showed them, in addition, what they should do in those fertile years of abundant crops and large harvests.

Another lesson: a person is not blamed for striving to remove an accusation from himself and to seek vindication for it; rather, he is praised for doing so. Yusuf refused to leave the prison until his innocence was made clear by the state of the women who had cut their hands.

Another lesson: the virtue of knowledge, including knowledge of the rulings and the Sharia, knowledge of dream interpretation, and knowledge of management and upbringing. Knowledge is better than outward beauty, even if that beauty reaches the level of Yusuf's beauty. Yusuf's beauty brought him that trial and imprisonment, while his knowledge brought him honour, elevation, and firm establishment in the land. Every good in this world and the Hereafter is a consequence and necessary result of knowledge.

Another lesson: the knowledge of interpreting dreams (*ta'bir al-ru'ya*) is among the Sharia sciences, and a person is rewarded for learning and teaching it. Dream interpretation falls under giving a ruling (*fatwa*), as shown by His words to the two young men, "The matter about which you both seek a ruling has been decided" (﴿قُضِيَ الأمرُ الذي فيه تستفتيان﴾). The king said, "Give me a ruling about my dream" (﴿أفتوني في رؤيايَ﴾), and the young man said to Yusuf, "Give us a ruling about seven fat cows..." (﴿أفۡتِنا في سبع بقراتٍ﴾), and the verses that follow. Therefore, it is not permissible to undertake interpreting a dream without knowledge.

Another lesson: there is no harm in a person describing what he has of the attributes of perfection, whether in knowledge or in action, when there is a benefit in doing so, provided he does not intend showing off (*riya'*) and remains free of falsehood. Yusuf said, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian" (﴿اجعَلۡني على خزائن الأرض إنِّي حفيظٌ عليمٌ﴾).

Likewise, holding public office is not blameworthy when the one who holds it fulfils, to the extent of his ability, the rights of God and the rights of His servants. There is no harm in seeking it when the one seeking it is more qualified than others. What is blameworthy is seeking office when one lacks the competence for it, or when someone else of similar or higher standing exists, or when one does not intend by it to establish the command of God. For these reasons, seeking office and exposing oneself to it are forbidden.

Another lesson: God is vast in generosity and munificence. He bestows upon His servant the good of this world and the Hereafter. The good of the Hereafter has two causes: faith (*iman*) and piety (*taqwa*). It is better than the reward and possession of this world. A servant should encourage his soul and make it long for God's reward, and should not let it grieve when it sees the people of this world and their pleasures while it is unable to obtain them. Rather, he should console it with God's reward in the Hereafter and His great bounty, as He says, "And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of God" (﴿ولأجۡرُ الآخرة خيرٌ للذين آمنوا وكانوا يتَّقون﴾).

Another lesson: collecting provisions and food is permissible when its aim is to extend provision to people without harming them. Yusuf commanded them to gather grain and food in the fertile years in preparation for the lean years. This does not contradict reliance upon God (*tawakkul*). Rather, the servant relies upon God while also acting upon the means that benefit him in his religion and his worldly life.

Another lesson: the excellent management of Yusuf when he took charge of the storehouses of the land, so that the stores of grain became very abundant. People from distant regions came to Egypt seeking provisions, because they knew the grain was plentiful there. He would not measure out to anyone more than the amount of their specific need, or less than that, and he did not give any arrival more than the measure of a camel's load.

Another lesson: the legitimacy of hospitality (*diyafa*), that it is one of the traditions of the messengers, and that honouring the guest is recommended. This is shown by Yusuf's words to his brothers, "Do you not see that I give full measure, and that I am the best of hosts?" (﴿ألا تَرَوۡنَ أنِّي أوفي الكيل وأنا خيرُ المنزِلينَ﴾).

Another lesson: having bad thoughts (*su' al-zann*) when there are clear indications for them is not forbidden or prohibited. Jacob refused to send Yusuf with them until they pressed him very hard, and then, after they came to him and claimed that a wolf had devoured Yusuf, he said, "Rather, your souls have beautified a matter for you" (﴿بل سوَّلت لكم أنفسُكم أمراً﴾). He said to them about the other brother, "Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?" (﴿هل آمَنُكُم عليه إلاَّ كما أمِنتُكم على أخيه من قبل﴾). Then, when Yusuf detained his brother with him and his brothers came to their father without him, he said to them, "Rather, your souls have beautified a matter for you" (﴿بل سوَّلَتۡ لكم أنفسُكم أمراً﴾). In this latter case, although they were not negligent, what had occurred from them made it necessary for their father to say what he said, without sin or blame upon him.

Another lesson: using means that ward off the evil eye and other harms, or that remove them after they have befallen, is not forbidden but permissible, even though nothing happens except by God's decree and predestination (*qada' wa qadar*). Means are themselves part of God's decree and predestination. This is shown by Jacob's command to his sons, "O my sons, do not enter by one gate, but enter by different gates" (﴿يا بنيَّ لا تدخُلوا من بابٍ واحدٍ وادخلوا من أبواب متفرقة﴾).

Another lesson: the permissibility of using stratagems (*makayid*) by which rights may be attained. Knowing hidden methods that lead to one's goals is praiseworthy for the servant. What is forbidden is only devising a way to cancel an obligation or to commit a prohibited act.

Another lesson: a person who wishes to give another the impression of something he does not want the other to know should use indirect speech, whether verbal or practical (*ma'arid*), which prevents him from lying. This is what Yusuf did when he placed the bowl in his brother's bag, then took it out, giving the impression that he was a thief, while there was nothing in it except an indication that suggested this to his brothers. Afterwards he said, "God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property" (﴿معاذَ الله أن نأخُذَ إلاَّ مَن وجدنا متاعنا عنده﴾). He did not say, "Whoever stole our property," nor did he say, "We found our property with him." Rather, he used a general statement that suits him and others. There is no prohibition in this. It only gives the impression that he is a thief, in order to achieve the immediate aim, which was that his brother would remain with him. This false impression was removed from the brother after the situation became clear.

Another lesson: a person may testify only to what he knows and has verified, either through direct observation or through the report of someone he trusts and whose report reassures the soul. This is shown by their words, "We bear witness only to what we know" (﴿وما شَهِدۡنا إلا بما علمنا﴾).

Another lesson: this great trial by which God tested His prophet and chosen one, Jacob, peace be upon him. God decreed that he be separated from his son Yusuf, whom he could not bear to be parted from even for one hour, and this separation grieved him most intensely. The separation lasted a long time, not less than thirty years, and sorrow never left Jacob's heart during that period. "His eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing it" (﴿وابيضَّتۡ عيناه من الحزنِ فهو كظيمٌ﴾). Then the matter grew even more severe when he was separated from his second son, Yusuf's full brother. Yet he remained patient with God's command, seeking his reward from God. He had pledged to himself beautiful patience, and there is no doubt that he fulfilled what he pledged. His words, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God" (﴿إنَّما أشكو بثِّي وحزني إلى الله﴾), do not contradict this, for complaining to God does not contradict patience. What contradicts it is complaining to created beings.

Another lesson: relief comes with distress, and with hardship comes ease. When Jacob's grief lasted long and grew intense to its utmost limit, and then the family of Jacob fell into dire need and harm touched them, God then permitted relief. The reunion came at the most critical time of their need and necessity, so the reward was completed and joy came. It is known from this that God tests His friends with hardship and ease, with adversity and prosperity, in order to test their patience and gratitude, and thereby their faith, certainty, and knowledge of Him increase.

Another lesson: a person may inform others of what he is experiencing, such as illness, poverty, or similar things, without complaining bitterly (*tasakhkhut*). Yusuf's brothers said, "O Chief, adversity has afflicted us and our family" (﴿يا أيُّها العزيز مسَّنا وأهلَنا الضرُّ﴾), and Yusuf did not object to them.

Another lesson: the virtue of piety and patience, and that every good in this world and the Hereafter is a consequence of piety and patience, and that the outcome for those who possess them is the best outcome. This is shown by His words, "God has been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever is mindful of God and patient, God does not waste the reward of the doers of good" (﴿قد منَّ الله علينا إنَّه من يتَّقِ ويَصۡبِرۡ فإنَّ الله لا يضيع أجر المحسنين﴾).

Another lesson: whoever has been blessed by God with a blessing after hardship, poverty, and a bad condition should acknowledge God's blessing upon him and should not stop remembering his former state, so that this remembrance produces gratitude whenever he recalls it. This is shown by Yusuf's words, peace be upon him, "He was good to me when He brought me out of prison and brought you from the desert" (﴿وقد أحسنَ بي إذ أخرَجَني من السجن وجاء بكم من البَدۡوِ﴾).

Another lesson: the great kindness of God toward Yusuf, in that He transferred him through those conditions and brought him hardships and trials, so that through them He might bring him to the highest goals and the loftiest ranks.

Another lesson: a servant should constantly turn to God, seeking to have his faith firmly established, should adopt the means that bring this about, and should ask God for a good ending and the completion of His blessing. This is shown by the words of Yusuf, peace be upon him, "My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom and taught me the interpretation of dreams. Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Let me die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous" (﴿ربِّي قد آتَيۡتَني من الملك وعلَّمۡتني من تأويل الأحاديث فاطر السمواتِ والأرض أنتَ وليِّي في الدُّنيا والآخرة توفَّني مسلماً وألحقۡني بالصَّالحين﴾).

This is what God has facilitated of benefits and lessons in this blessed story. Surely other things will become apparent to the one who reflects and contemplates. We ask Him, exalted is He, for beneficial knowledge and accepted deeds, for He is Generous and Bountiful.

The commentary on Surah Yusuf, and his father and brothers, peace be upon them, is complete. All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds.
